prime.problem: HumanEval+ runs about 764 tests per task for every sample of every model, which is slow. Cutting tests at random could drop the one test that catches a particular bug, and then scores rise again for no reason.
prime.fits: Mutation testing gave each test a kill set. This card treats those sets, plus branch coverage and other models' sample kills, as requirements, and keeps the fewest tests that still meet all of them.
prime.goal: Run greedy set cover by hand, explain what the reduction preserves and what it doesn't, and read table 4 to see which requirement does the work.

attend: What exactly does reduction promise to keep, stated in terms of requirements rather than tests?
Why is the greedy choice "most still-uncovered requirements" rather than "most requirements in total"?
Why is the exact smallest cover not computed, and how much does greedy give up?
In table 4, which single requirement already lands near the full HumanEval+ result, and what does it cost in tests?
Why is mini slightly more lenient than the full suite, and in which direction does that bias scores?

must: Each test satisfies a set of requirements (branches, killed mutants, killed samples) → keep a subset that still satisfies every requirement the full suite met → reduction becomes set cover → 764.1 tests shrink to 16.1 (47×)
Exact set cover is NP-hard → greedy repeatedly takes the test adding the most uncovered requirements → fast and within about a ln n factor of optimal, the best practical guarantee
Only requirements are preserved → a bug no branch, mutant or recorded sample ever exposed can lose its catching test → mini is slightly lenient (GPT-4 78.0 vs 76.2)
Coverage and mutants alone keep few tests but leave GPT-4 at 86.0 and 82.9 → real sample kills bring it to 78.7 → merging all three gives 78.0 with 16.1 tests
elevated: Sample kills come from models' wrong outputs → using a model's own kills would fit the suite to it → the paper builds each model's reduced suite without that model (leave-one-out)
reference: tie-breaking order in the worked example

compress.prompt: From memory, explain reduction in 3–4 sentences: what the requirements are, how greedy picks tests, what is guaranteed, and what is not. Then redo the three greedy rounds for T1–T4.
checklist: requirements: branches covered, mutants killed, other models' samples killed
keep a subset meeting every requirement the full suite met (set cover)
greedy: take the test with most uncovered requirements, repeat
result: 16.1 tests per task, 47× fewer, nearly the same verdict
not guaranteed: bugs outside the chosen requirements

retrieve.q: Explain why reduction by requirements is safer than keeping a random 2% of the tests.
answer: random sampling can drop the only test that catches a given bug
requirement-based reduction keeps at least one test for every requirement met
so the bugs represented by those requirements stay caught

retrieve.q: Run greedy on T1–T4 with the tie in round 1 broken the other way (T4 before T2). Which tests are picked, and is the result still 3 tests?
answer: round 1: T4 covers M3, M4 → uncovered {M1, M2}
round 2: T2 (M1) and T3 (M2) each add 1; take either
round 3: take the other; still 3 tests, all 4 mutants killed

retrieve.q: When would you insist on the full HumanEval+ suite instead of mini, even though mini is 47× cheaper?
answer: when you need the strict number for a paper or leaderboard (mini runs about 1.8 points high for GPT-4)
when evaluating a new model whose failure modes the pool of models never showed
when run time isn't the bottleneck

compare.q: Reduction decides which tests exist in mini; leave-one-out decides whose kills may be used to make that decision. What goes wrong with reduction alone, and what does leave-one-out cost?
answer: alone, a model's own wrong samples would guarantee the tests that catch it survive
so its mini score would match the full suite by construction
leave-one-out builds one reduced suite per model, 19 reductions instead of 1
and still can't cover failure modes no other model had

compare.q: Coverage alone gives 11.3 tests and GPT-4 86.0; the merged requirements give 16.1 tests and 78.0. Which design choice makes the difference, and what would you lose by dropping coverage from the merge?
answer: merging adds mutant and sample-kill requirements that coverage can't see
those keep tests that detect wrong outputs, not just execute branches
dropping coverage loses the guarantee that every branch is still exercised, even if few tests are saved

predict.q: Greedy isn't always optimal. Take requirements {1, …, 6} and three tests: Y1 = {1, 2, 3}, Y2 = {4, 5, 6}, G = {1, 2, 4, 5}. Commit: how many tests does greedy keep, and what is the true minimum?
predict.answer: Greedy takes G first (4 new), then needs Y1 for 3 and Y2 for 6: 3 tests. The minimum is 2 (Y1 + Y2). The test that covers the most at first can be a trap. Greedy's ln n bound says how bad this can get; in practice it is close enough that the paper uses it.

apply.task: Merge requirements the way EvalPlus does. Give each is_prime test the union of its branches (from the branch-coverage card: T1 {b1}, T2 {b2, b4}, T3 {b2, b3, b5}, T4 {b2, b3, b4, b6}) and its mutant kills (T1 {}, T2 {M1, M4}, T3 {M2}, T4 {M3, M4}). Run greedy round by round, writing each test's new-requirement count. Then say which test survives only because of branches and which only because of mutants.
apply.done: Round 1: T4 (6 new). Round 2: T3 (2 new: b5, M2). Round 3: T1 or T2 (1 each). Round 4: the other. All four tests are kept. T1 survives only for b1 (mutation alone dropped it), and T2 only for M1 (coverage alone dropped it).
apply.hint: Before round 1 the counts are T1 1, T2 4, T3 4, T4 6.
